citation: Zhou Y, Zhang X, Wang J (2026). Post-activation potentiation enhancement induction strategies with different rest intervals on jump performance: a meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology.
population: Healthy individuals aged 11–43 years (undergraduate students or athletes in football, track and field, etc.), mixed genders, 468 participants across 22 RCTs
intervention: Post-activation potentiation enhancement (PAPE) induction methods including back squat, squat, running, isometric contractions, and plyometric exercises, with rest intervals of 2–20 minutes
summary: This meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (468 participants) found that post-activation potentiation enhancement (PAPE) significantly improves jump performance (SMD = 1.36, 95% CI 0.89–1.83, p < 0.0001). Subgroup analyses indicated the largest effects for back squat induction (SMD = 2.85), male participants (SMD = 1.53), counter-movement jump outcomes (SMD = 1.34), moderate exercise intensity (SMD = 2.46), and rest intervals of 3–7 minutes (SMD = 1.47).
key_findings: Overall pooled effect: SMD = 1.36, 95% CI (0.89, 1.83), P < 0.0001, indicating PAPE significantly improves jump performance.
Back squat induction yielded the largest effect size: SMD = 2.85, 95% CI (0.98, 4.73), P = 0.003.
Male subgroup showed larger effect than female: SMD = 1.53, 95% CI (0.92, 2.14), P < 0.0001.
Moderate-intensity PAPE produced the largest effect: SMD = 2.46, 95% CI (1.71, 3.22), P < 0.0001.
Rest interval of 3–7 minutes gave the largest effect: SMD = 1.47, 95% CI (0.79, 2.14), P < 0.0001.
limitations: Substantial heterogeneity (I² = 51%) across studies; many included RCTs had high risk of bias in allocation concealment and blinding. Sensitivity analysis showed results were stable but heterogeneity remained moderate.
